# Your AI agents are cooking your Mac.

Claude Code, Codex and Cursor start builds, tests and renders that turn a MacBook into a stove. WhoIsCooking lives in your notch, shows which agent is the heat, and cools it down without stopping its work.

Buy for $5

One-time purchase, no subscription. For Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 14 or later.

## Same render. 64°C before, 50°C after. [...] Recognises Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Aider, Copilot CLI, Ollama and LM Studio, plus Xcode builds, ffmpeg, Docker and your browser. Lives in the notch or the menu bar, whichever you prefer.

## Questions

Does cooling slow my agents down?

A bit. The work runs on the cooler efficiency cores, so it takes longer but stays quiet. Full speed puts everything back instantly, and quitting the app always restores full speed.

 Will it break my agent sessions?

No. It never freezes your terminal or your apps. It only changes which cores the work runs on, or quits something when you explicitly choose Quit.

 Does the app itself heat my Mac? [...] ## Same render. 64°C before, 50°C after.

Cooling moves heavy work onto your Mac's efficiency cores. The job keeps running, a little slower, and your Mac drops about 14 degrees. Click Full speed whenever you want the power back.

### One row per agent

An agent session and everything it started (builds, tests, dev servers, renders) shows up as a single line, instead of 80 cryptic processes.

### Cool, don't kill

Nothing gets frozen or closed unless you ask. Your terminal and your apps stay usable the whole time.

### Knows when something runs away

You get a nudge when an agent burns CPU for five minutes straight, or leaves dev servers running after its session ends.

Hi Product Hunt, I'm Andrew, the maker.

I run Claude Code and Codex on a MacBook and it kept getting hot, with no way to tell which agent was responsible. Activity Monitor shows dozens of node and compiler processes and no temperature at all.

WhoIsCooking shows the chip temperature in your notch or menu bar, groups each agent session with everything it started into one row, and has a "Cool down my Mac" button that moves busy work to the efficiency cores. Nothing is killed or frozen. On my M5, 4 processes flat out went from about 83°C at full speed to about 48°C cooled. The work just runs a bit slower.

Honest limits: it can't cool GPU work or Apple's own processes, and it needs Apple Silicon (M1 to M5) on macOS 14+. [...] It's $5 one time, signed and notarized, no account. I'd love feedback on what else it should show per agent.

## FAQs

### How do I cool down my Mac?

To cool down your Mac and prevent overheating, you can try the following steps: [...] Delete unnecessary files: Delete all unnecessary files — cleaning up your Mac is essential to maintaining its performance.
 Close resource-intensive apps: Quit any programs that are putting a heavy load on your Mac's processor. This will reduce the strain on your system and help it cool down.
 Limit the number of browser tabs open: Having too many tabs open in your web browser can consume a significant amount of system resources. Close unnecessary tabs to reduce the strain on your Mac.
 Place your Mac on a hard, flat surface: Ensure that your Mac is placed on a solid, flat surface that allows proper airflow. Avoid using it on soft surfaces like beds or couches, as that can block ventilation and lead to overheating.
